Understanding the Risk Environment: What Shapes Renewable Investment?
M5: Derisking Renewable Energy Investment (DREI)
Lesson 2 Overview
In this section, you will learn about the specific risk environment that shapes renewable energy investment.

Building on earlier discussions of financing structures and capital costs, you will look more closely at how different categories of risk interact with investment decisions and influence project bankability.

You will explore the main types of risks most relevant for renewable energy projects in developing countries and see how these risks affect the cost of capital and overall competitiveness.

You will also examine practical approaches to addressing risks, including both private and public derisking strategies, and learn how the DREI framework helps policymakers identify effective instruments for improving investment conditions.

By the end of this section, you will understand how risks are assessed, how they influence financing outcomes, and what tools and strategies can be applied to create a more predictable and attractive investment environment for renewable energy.
M5: Derisking Renewable Energy Investment (DREI)
A: The Risk Landscape: Concepts and Analytical Approaches
In the beginning of the DREI process, attention is placed on understanding the overall investment risk environment for a selected renewable energy technology.
This stage helps to identify the barriers that prevent private actors from investing at scale and at affordable financing terms.

It combines stakeholder engagement, structured research, and quantitative tools to produce a clear and actionable picture of investment risk in the national context.

The process typically begins with market research and preliminary workshops with public actors, including government agencies, regulators, and utilities.
These early engagements help frame the country’s energy sector context, define the technology focus (e.g.

wind, solar PV, mini-grids), and align on the scope and objectives of the DREI process.

Following this, the derisking table is tailored to the specific national and technological situation.

The table is structured around ten standard DREI investment risk categories—such as power market risk, permitting risk, or political risk—and breaks each category down into detailed barriers, relevant stakeholders, and potential public instruments that could mitigate them.
This process ensures that the analysis reflects local institutional, market, and regulatory realities.
The next step involves structured interviews with private sector stakeholders, such as developers, financiers, and service providers.
These interviews serve as the main channel for assessing the perceived severity of each investment risk.
Interviewees provide scores and qualitative observations for each risk category and are also invited to propose appropriate derisking instruments.
Importantly, they are asked to estimate the cost of equity and debt they would expect under current conditions, offering a grounded view of financing expectations.
<strong>All data from the structured interviews feed into the Financing Costs Tool.
This tool aggregates the information to estimate the total cost of capital (weighted average cost of capital, or WACC) for the selected technology.
The main output is the Financing Costs Waterfall, which visually presents the contribution of each risk category to the overall financing cost.
This output is especially useful for policy makers in identifying priority areas for public intervention and understanding how different risks affect investment viability.
M5: Derisking Renewable Energy Investment (DREI)
B: Application example
The DREI methodology for assessing the risk environment has been applied in multiple contexts across technologies and regions.

Kenya provides two practical examples of its application—one in utility-scale wind and another in off-grid solar mini-grids.

In the 2013 DREI study, Kenya was included as one of the case studies for utility-scale wind power.
The analysis involved in-country engagement and structured interviews with project developers and financial institutions.
It identified key risk categories such as power market risk, related to the off-taker’s financial stability, and permitting risk, linked to land acquisition and environmental clearances.

The Financing Costs Waterfall for Kenya highlighted the significant cost contribution of these risks to the cost of capital for <ai prompt="Clarify wind energy.">wind energy 💬️</ai>, providing a foundation for targeted derisking recommendations.

In the 2018 DREI Off-grid Electrification report, Kenya was again selected, this time for an application focused on solar PV-battery mini-grids. The context here was rural electrification, where projects face high upfront costs and limited ability to pay among users.

Structured interviews revealed prominent risks including demand risk, due to uncertain load profiles; regulatory risk, due to unclear licensing requirements; and access-to-finance risk, due to the scarcity of long-term credit.

The resulting Financing Costs Waterfall showed how these risks inflated financing costs, reinforcing the need for targeted interventions such as regulatory reforms and concessional lending mechanisms.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Use the Derisking Table to See the Whole Picture of Your Sector
The investigation of the risk environment starts with the understanding of the sector’s dynamics, actors and potential for development.

This initial evaluation supports the tailoring of the “Derisking Table”, that lists all possible barriers underlying the risk categories of each technology, as well as the relevant stakeholders and the possible derisking instruments.
Talk to Private Actors to Understand How Risks Are Really Felt
Structured interviews with private actors active in the sector are the main source of information on the risk perception of the different actors.
They provide scores and qualitative considerations on the different risks and their underlying barriers and the potential instruments that may be implemented to reduce them.
They are also asked to provide estimates of cost of equity and loans.
Use the Financing Costs Waterfall to See How Risks Drive Up Capital Costs

The main output of this stage of the methodology consists of the Financing Costs Waterfall, that presents estimates of the impact of each risk category on the cost of capital for the technology in the country where the study is developed.
